utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome. May I suggest there is something which we perhaps better have very clear perhaps by agreement. What is the colour of the old JNA uniform?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Domazet has done service in the People's Yugoslav Army, so I would rely on his representation of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What is it, Mr. Domazet? What is the colour? Let's hear it from the horse's mouth. I'm sorry. That's a colloquialism that you may not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the colour of the uniform was described with an acronym, SMB, which stands for grey/olive-green uniform. It was a unicoloured uniform and of the lighter shade of olive-green colour. That was the customary and the only uniform at the time when I did my military service. Later on, in addition to this particular uniform, a camouflage uniform was introduced, but unlike these other police camouflage uniforms, the JNA camouflage uniform has some brown and reddish hues and it has this characteristic pattern, whereas the police camouflage uniform is blue and not as multicoloured as the military one. I don't know if this is of any assistance to you, Your Honours. If this should be challenged, I think that we can present additional evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think it's fair to say, Mr. Domazet, that was my understanding of it, but there have been a number of witnesses, including this one, who have referred to it without describing the colour, and I thought we had better get it straight. Have you got any objection to any of the descriptions that Mr. Domazet gave, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No. I accept Mr. Domazet's representation of the uniforms to the extent that they do not contradict the witness. If the witness describes different colours, I would ask the Court to rely on what the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No. This witness made it very clear what she meant, and it was the same as Mr. Domazet's description, but I thought we should have it on the record somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, have you got any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions. Re-examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 101, Mr. Domazet asked you about describing the column of people as it came up Pionirska Street from the town to the big house. I want to ask you a question about that column. My question is: Are you able to approximate the length of the column, that is, the distance from the first person in the group of people to the last person in the group of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG101
utterances.text: I don't know exactly the column --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We're having difficulty hearing the witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG101
utterances.text: We were in a column two by two, moving towards Pionirska Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the group of people were two people side by side, for whatever length that took; is that correct? I saw you nod your head. Would you please answer verbally.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG101
utterances.text: No. I don't know how long it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But are you saying that the column, the width of the column, was only two people wide, one person next to another?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG101
utterances.text: Yes, two by two, maybe three in cases of some women with children, like a woman leading her two children, but mostly it was two by two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by the time this column was on Pionirska Street, what is your best estimate of how many people were in the column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG101
utterances.text: Fifty-three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you approximate for us where in this column you were? Were you at the front, at the rear, somewhere in the middle? Can you approximate where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG101
utterances.text: No. No, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Domazet asked you about a person by the name of Mujo Jasarevic, and in answer to one of his questions you stated that this man knew Mitar Vasiljevic very well. My question to you is: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG101
utterances.text: I think that in that house either Mujo or Alija would have known that, because in that village, Mitar's wife, Milojka, also worked, and they were there together in that shop. I don't know whether it was Mujo or Alija. One of them or both of them liked to drink. Other people knew him very well. He even addressed a woman from our village. He spoke to her about her brother, who had been taken away at the very beginning. He told her that he was safe, that he was in Sarajevo, that she should not worry. She was also one of the people who knew him very well. She used to work in Visegrad, and she told us that Mitar had told her that her brother had been taken to Sarajevo and that he was safe and that we would also reach Kladanj in safety and that she would be reunited with her brother, that he was alive and well. However, ever since the beginning of the war, no one has ever heard about that man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, on the 14th of June, ever hear Mujo Jasarevic refer to Mitar Vasiljevic, using his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG101
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that while I was in the house, but I also heard it from other people who knew him very well, in particular, this woman I just told you about. She knew him. She even spoke to him when he told her about her brother, that he was safe, that they should not worry about him, that he would be transferred to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness 101. That is all the questions I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, madam, for giving evidence before the Tribunal today and for the evidence you gave. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that the last of the witnesses on videolink?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, there's probably little opportunity to start another witness this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME

utterances.text: Have you got one here?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There is one here, but may I suggest we discuss the subpoenaed witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have some updated information regarding them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. We will deal with the next witness tomorrow. We will only be sitting until lunchtime tomorrow, unless there's only a tiny bit of evidence to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The information that I have at this point is that both of the witnesses have agreed to come up. They apparently went to apply for passports today and for their visa applications today. However, the earliest that that process will be completed would bring them here or make them available to testify at the very end of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's all right. Your last witness, I gather, is Dr. de Grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So that you've got the Friday and the Monday to fill in even on your -- I think this is the penultimate version of the -- the new one, yes. Yes, even on the most recent edition of your schedule, you've got Friday and Monday to fill in, so that should do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It does not matter if the case goes on past Dr. de Grave but I just have to keep in mind a few other matters that are happening around at that time. One of them is that on that Friday, that will be Friday the -- I'm sorry. Go back one. Thursday, the 11th of October, all of the Judges of the Tribunal are travelling to a conference elsewhere in Europe with the Rwanda Tribunal. This is an annual event that we're expected to attend and we'll be leaving sometime during the course of the afternoon, depending upon the amount of time we have to be at the airport before the plane leaves, which at the moment I'm told is three hours, rather an alarming prospect. So that Thursday and obviously the Friday of that week, we will not be available, Thursday afternoon at least. Very well, then. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just one small matter on this. It will be until tomorrow -- we won't be able to have the next week's witness to the Court until tomorrow afternoon. There are some problems, logistical problems. We will have witnesses here next week, but we're not sure which order. As soon as we can get that finalised we'll get that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The most important person you should notify, of course, is Mr. Domazet, because he has to be ready to cross-examine them, and my own experience of it is that you like to have the evening before with the witnesses you know are going to be called the next day, otherwise from the Trial Chamber's point of view it doesn't matter. Very well. We'll adjourn now until 9.30 tomorrow.
